text: Flick has made that question harder by using Raphinha as the central forward. It sounds like a simple positional switch. It is not. A conventional nine often gives defenders a reference point: the striker in front of them, the winger outside them. Raphinha blurs both references. He can start between the center backs, dart across one shoulder, drift away to combine, then arrive in the box as the last man defenders expect to meet. He has the acceleration of a wide attacker and the urgency of a striker hunting the finish. Against Feyenoord, Pedri's pass released one of those central runs. Against Sevilla, Christensen's pass found another. These are different games, but the same defensive hesitation: step out early and leave space behind; wait, and Raphinha is already moving through it. That is why the new role changes more than his personal scoring column. He also brings an old winger instinct to this central job. He likes arriving at speed rather than standing still, so an apparently quiet spell can end with one movement that changes the geometry of the box.
